title: Dispatch: Setting Up Secret Courts
gist: The Alien Terrorist Removal Court, created in 1996 and dormant for 30 years, heard its first-ever case on July 30 when the Justice Department's National Security Division moved to deport Afghan lawful permanent resident Nazira Haji Zada on classified evidence. The dispatch documents an institution being improvised in real time — a website hastily posted, an electronic filing system not yet built, a judge warning of ineloquence — with the central fight already joined over whether the government must give cleared defense counsel access to the classified record under 8 U.S.C. § 1534.

insights.claim: The Alien Terrorist Removal Court, established in 1996, received no case for 30 years until Justice Department National Security Division officials asked a judge to remove a noncitizen suspected of terrorist ties from the United States.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Dormant statutory authorities can be switched on without new legislation — a template for executive action that bypasses the ordinary immigration and criminal systems.
insights.quote: the court, established in 1996, has never received a case until now
insights.locator: Three documents trickle onto the website

insights.claim: The ATRC's existence surfaced publicly only when a hastily created website appeared late on the evening of Friday, July 17, sending journalists scrambling to determine what the court does.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Institutional activation with near-zero public notice means monitoring obscure government websites, not press releases, is where this beat is covered.
insights.quote: a hastily created website for the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC) appears, sending us journalists scrambling to figure out what a court we never had heard of does
insights.locator: And then one does.

insights.claim: Chief Judge Joan Ericksen, whose day job is senior judge in the District of Minnesota, opened the ATRC's first hearing by reading prepared remarks acknowledging the court is in the early stage of implementing procedures and warning there may be moments of ineloquence.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A judge openly conceding procedural improvisation signals a high near-term appellate reversal risk and years of unsettled process.
insights.quote: This is the court’s first case, and the court is in the early stage of implementing procedures
insights.locator: Reading from prepared remarks, Judge Ericksen says

insights.claim: The ATRC lacked basic court infrastructure at its first hearing, with clerks only beginning to build an electronic filing system and the government's lead counsel having to ask on the record how documents should be numbered on the docket.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the institution is being assembled during live proceedings against a detained respondent, which is itself a due process argument.
insights.locator: Just before he sits back down, O’Byrne asks how the court

insights.claim: ATRC filings will be free to access, breaking from the PACER norm of charging for federal court records.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Free docket access means this secretive court will paradoxically be one of the most closely and cheaply watched — expect heavy real-time coverage of every filing.
insights.quote: ATRC filings will not cost money to access, a break from norms under PACER
insights.locator: One difference—to the glee of much of the press corps

insights.claim: Public and press attention to the first hearing was thin, with the reporter fourth in line behind an NPR correspondent, a law clerk, and an NBC intern, reflecting D.C.'s shrinking ranks of legal journalists.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Declining legal-press capacity means precedent-setting national security proceedings can now unfold with minimal public scrutiny.
insights.quote: D.C.’s shrinking ranks of legal journalists
insights.locator: I’m fourth in line for a seat

insights.claim: The first ATRC respondent is Nazira Haji Zada, a 47-year-old Afghan citizen and lawful permanent resident arrested by the FBI in Fort Worth, Texas on July 28, whom the government seeks to deport to Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The government chose a lawful permanent resident, not an undocumented entrant, for its first test case — the strongest possible due process posture for the defense.
insights.locator: Two deputies with the U.S. Marshals Service escort

insights.claim: The government alleges Haji Zada pledged loyalty to the Islamic State and supported a conspiracy to conduct a mass attack on Election Day 2024 with her son and son-in-law, who were arrested in October 2024, with the son now serving a maximum 15-year sentence after pleading guilty to the plot.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A related criminal conviction already exists in the family, raising the question of why the government chose civil removal on classified evidence instead of prosecution.
insights.locator: He reads the unclassified summary nearly verbatim

insights.claim: The government further alleges Haji Zada went to great lengths to indoctrinate her children into ISIS ideology and relocate them to ISIS-controlled territory, concealing the plan from her husband, an Afghan man who previously worked at Bagram Air Base.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The family's Bagram connection ties this case to the broader Afghan evacuee vetting debate, a likely vector for policy escalation.
insights.locator: O’Byrne also alleges that Haji Zada has gone

insights.claim: The government's public description of its case was so terse that Chief Judge Ericksen had to ask lead counsel Hayden O'Byrne three separate times, finally specifying in plain English, to actually state the allegations Haji Zada faces.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Judicial impatience with government opacity at the very first hearing is an early signal the court will not simply rubber-stamp classification claims.
insights.quote: Unsatisfied, Ericksen asks him a third time to tell Haji Zada about the allegations she faces, this time adding “in plain English.”
insights.locator: O’Byrne is terse in his description of the allegations

insights.claim: The details of how Haji Zada supported a plot foiled almost two years earlier, or of her efforts to support ISIS, remain murky at best even after the government's unclassified summary was read aloud in open court.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The evidentiary gap between allegation and disclosure is the core structural feature of this court, and the thing appellate review will turn on.
insights.quote: the details about how Haji Zada supported a plot that was foiled almost two years ago, or her efforts to support ISIS, are murky at best
insights.locator: Judge Ericksen leaves it at that

insights.claim: Neither the government's lead national security counsel, the other prosecutors present, nor defense counsel knew whether Afghanistan is a mandatory consular reporting country, forcing the judge to read both alternative statements of law aloud.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Basic preparedness gaps in the government's first-ever case in this forum suggest the activation was rushed rather than long-planned.
insights.locator: She moves on to ask whether O’Byrne knows

insights.claim: The ATRC's design allows the government to introduce classified and warrantless evidence without even the respondent's knowledge, which will keep most answers about the case permanently out of public reach.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Defines the forum's core asymmetry: outcomes will be largely unreviewable in public, so procedural rulings are the only observable signal.
insights.quote: allowing the government to introduce classified and warrantless evidence without even the respondent’s knowledge
insights.locator: The court’s secretive nature

insights.claim: The Justice Department has indicated it will not share classified materials with Haji Zada's counsel, despite the ATRC statute entitling a lawful permanent resident to an attorney with a security clearance who can access and contest that information on her behalf.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: This is the case's decisive legal fight; a government win would effectively make the ATRC a one-party proceeding and invite constitutional challenge.
insights.locator: My ears perk up when Farley mentions

insights.claim: Chief Judge Ericksen stated her presumption is that the federal defender's office will be able to review classified evidence and that the government would need a pretty strong reason to change her mind, while also demanding a specific rationale for protecting each individual piece of classified information.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The presiding judge is leaning against blanket secrecy, which raises the odds the first ATRC case produces an adversarial record rather than an ex parte removal.
insights.quote: She says her presumption will be that the federal defender’s office will be able to review classified evidence and will need a “pretty strong reason” to change her mind.
insights.locator: Apparently, I’m not alone.

insights.claim: Ericksen warned she would not allow a unilateral classified mandate to conceal information from Haji Zada and cited the ATRC statute at 8 U.S.C. § 1534, which she read as giving the respondent's cleared counsel a right to access classified materials.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The specific statutory hook to track — how § 1534 is construed here sets the operating rules for every future ATRC case.
insights.quote: Ericksen warns that she won’t allow a unilateral classified mandate to conceal information from Haji Zada.
insights.locator: The judge tells O’Byrne that she expects the government

insights.claim: The government countered by invoking a subsection permitting a removal hearing to proceed without any unclassified summary if the judge finds that both the noncitizen's presence in the U.S. and provision of the summary would likely cause serious and irreparable harm to national security or death or serious bodily injury.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A statutory escape hatch that would let removal proceed with no disclosure at all — the maximalist government position now on the record.
insights.quote: likely cause serious and irreparable harm to the national security or death or serious bodily injury
insights.locator: After this, O’Byrne specifically points to a subsection

insights.claim: The government offered only 177 pages of discovery to Haji Zada's counsel, a very low number compared to discovery in most national security prosecutions, while asserting it is not relying entirely on classified information.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A hard quantitative marker of how thin the unclassified record is — 177 pages is the benchmark against which the classified case will be judged.
insights.quote: offers to turn over 177 pages of discovery to Haji Zada’s counsel at the hearing
insights.locator: Then, O’Byrne points out that the ATRC’s statute

insights.claim: An attorney who discloses classified information to their client in ATRC proceedings faces a mandatory minimum 10-year prison sentence under the ATRC statute.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A criminal penalty aimed at defense lawyers is an extreme chilling mechanism unique to this forum and likely a target of constitutional attack.
insights.quote: An attorney who discloses such information to their client in ATRC proceedings faces a mandatory minimum 10-year prison sentence, per the ATRC statute.
insights.locator: According to the ATRC statute, as a lawful permanent resident

insights.claim: Ericksen said she plans to proceed with a CIPA model in mind, importing the Classified Information Procedures Act framework used in criminal cases, which she noted has quite a robust history, into a civil removal proceeding.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Borrowing criminal-procedure safeguards into a civil forum is the judge's chosen legitimacy strategy and the most consequential procedural ruling so far.
insights.quote: proceed with a CIPA model in mind
insights.locator: Regarding the classified evidence in the case

insights.claim: Federal defender Matthew Farley moved immediately to dismiss the hearing and release Haji Zada, objecting that the ATRC's lack of process and due process is woefully inadequate.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The constitutional challenge was filed at the first possible moment, meaning appellate review of the ATRC's validity is likely within months.
insights.quote: calling the ATRC’s “lack of process and due process woefully inadequate.”
insights.locator: Next, federal defender Farley approaches the lectern

insights.claim: The defense characterized the ATRC as a runaround of bringing a criminal case in order to lower the standard of proof, framing the forum as a deliberate evasion of criminal procedure rather than a genuine immigration mechanism.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: If accepted, this framing would extend criminal due process protections to the whole forum and could shut it down again for another 30 years.
insights.quote: a runaround of bringing a criminal case
insights.locator: Farley says the ATRC functions as

insights.claim: Haji Zada's attorneys raised misgivings about the ATRC's constitutionality under the First, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Amendments, and will separately contest the adequacy of the government's unclassified summary, which consists of just a few paragraphs.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Four separate constitutional theories plus a statutory adequacy challenge give multiple independent paths to reversal — high litigation risk for the government's strategy.
insights.quote: citing the First, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Amendments
insights.locator: Continuing, Farley references the law reviews

insights.claim: Whether the case proceeds at all turns on Judge Ericksen ruling the government's unclassified summary adequate; if she finds it inadequate the case ends, subject only to a government appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A single adequacy ruling is the binary gate on the entire first ATRC case — the specific decision point to watch.
insights.quote: But, if Judge Ericksen finds it inadequate, the case will end, barring a successful government appeal
insights.locator: She instructs the Justice Department to submit a summary

insights.claim: The legal literature on the ATRC is so sparse that the presiding judge told defense counsel she had probably read the same law review articles as him because there aren't that many.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Near-total absence of precedent or scholarship means every ruling in this case becomes foundational law for the forum.
insights.quote: I’ve probably read the same law review articles as you. There aren’t that many.
insights.locator: Judge Ericksen chimes in with an earnest smile

insights.claim: Judge Ericksen denied the motion to release Haji Zada and folded the constitutional objections into a detention hearing scheduled for Aug. 11, while defense counsel argued they need a ruling on classified access before they can prepare for it.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Aug. 11 is the concrete next catalyst date, where both detention and the ATRC's constitutionality get argued together.
insights.locator: The judge denies Farley’s motion to release Haji Zada

insights.claim: Courts are normally products of law, transcripts, filings, and accumulated case law, making an institution that materializes overnight with no record behind it an anomaly worth treating as significant in itself.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Frames the durable takeaway: the existence and activation of secret adjudicative forums, not just their outcomes, is the thing to monitor.
insights.quote: Courts don’t just pop up out of nowhere.
insights.locator: Courts don’t just pop up out of nowhere.
